title: Jan 2019 (Abu Dhabi)
des: DOH (HAAD) paediatrics recall, Abu Dhabi exam January 2019. Answers checked and explained.

questions.question: A sexually active adolescent girl has had regular periods since puberty but no period for 8 weeks. She has no hirsutism and her breasts are mature. What is the most appropriate next test?
questions.exp: Pregnancy is the most common cause of secondary amenorrhoea in an adolescent who is sexually active, so a pregnancy test always comes first, before any other investigation. Then consider prolactin, TFTs, FSH/LH and androgens.

questions.question: An obese adolescent girl (BMI 36) has had irregular periods since puberty and hirsutism on the face and upper arms. There is a family history of type 2 diabetes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: PCOS: oligomenorrhoea plus clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne), often with obesity, insulin resistance (acanthosis nigricans) and a family history of type 2 diabetes. In adolescents, both irregular cycles (persisting beyond 2 years after menarche) and hyperandrogenism are needed. Rapid virilisation suggests a tumour; check 17-OHP for non-classical CAH.

questions.question: In the same girl with suspected polycystic ovary syndrome, which test best supports the diagnosis?
questions.exp: In adolescents, PCOS is diagnosed by irregular periods plus hyperandrogenism, ideally shown biochemically (raised total or free testosterone). Pelvic ultrasound is NOT recommended for diagnosis within 8 years of menarche, because multifollicular ovaries are normal at this age; it is used only to exclude other causes such as tumours. Also check TFTs, prolactin and 17-OHP to exclude mimics.

questions.question: What is the appropriate management for this obese adolescent with polycystic ovary syndrome?
questions.a: Lifestyle changes with diet and exercise, plus a combined oral contraceptive pill for the periods and hirsutism
questions.b: Metformin alone, with no lifestyle advice
questions.e: No treatment until she wants to become pregnant
questions.exp: Weight loss through diet and exercise is first-line in every overweight girl with PCOS: even 5–10% loss improves cycles and androgens. The combined oral contraceptive pill regulates periods, protects the endometrium and reduces hirsutism and acne. Metformin is added for insulin resistance or impaired glucose tolerance; anti-androgens (spironolactone) are added after 6 months of COCP if hirsutism persists, and need contraception.

questions.question: A sexually active adolescent girl has a purulent vaginal discharge and a red, inflamed vulva. She has had unprotected sex. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: A purulent (pus-like) discharge after unprotected sex suggests gonorrhoea (often with chlamydia, so test and treat both). Candida gives a thick white curd-like discharge with itching; bacterial vaginosis (Gardnerella) gives a thin grey fishy discharge without inflammation; HSV gives painful ulcers. Test with NAAT, treat with ceftriaxone, treat partners and screen for other STIs.

questions.question: Which test confirms the diagnosis of autoimmune haemolytic anaemia?
questions.exp: The direct antiglobulin test detects antibody (IgG) or complement (C3) already bound to the patient's red cells, which defines autoimmune haemolysis. The indirect Coombs test looks for free antibodies in serum (used in antenatal and cross-match testing). Osmotic fragility/EMA binding is for hereditary spherocytosis.

questions.question: A child has acute haemolysis with low haemoglobin and high reticulocytes. The direct Coombs test is positive for IgG, and the antibody reacts at body temperature (37°C). What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Warm AIHA: IgG antibodies that bind best at 37°C, causing extravascular haemolysis in the spleen, with spherocytes. Treat with steroids. Cold agglutinin disease is IgM (after Mycoplasma or EBV), active below 37°C, and fixes complement (C3 positive). Paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria (Donath–Landsteiner IgG antibody) follows viral infections in children.

questions.question: A child with sickle cell disease gets parvovirus B19 infection (fifth disease). What is he at risk of?
questions.exp: Parvovirus B19 infects red cell precursors and stops red cell production for 7–10 days. With the short red cell lifespan in sickle cell disease, Hb falls fast with a very low reticulocyte count (transient aplastic crisis). Treat with blood transfusion; recovery comes with returning reticulocytes. Isolate from pregnant staff and other patients with haemolytic anaemia.

questions.question: A newborn baby has petechiae. He is otherwise well and feeding normally, and the blood count shows thrombocytopenia. What is the most appropriate first step towards diagnosis?
questions.d: Take the maternal history and check the mother's platelet count
questions.exp: In a well neonate with thrombocytopenia, the cause is usually immune. A low maternal platelet count (or a history of ITP or lupus) points to maternal autoimmune thrombocytopenia; a normal maternal count points to neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia. A sick baby needs a sepsis screen.

questions.question: A child has recurrent prolonged fevers. Full blood count shows a white cell count of 6,000 with only 0.4% neutrophils. What is the most appropriate first step?
questions.b: Oral antibiotics and review in a week
questions.d: Wait for blood culture results before treating
questions.e: Bone marrow biopsy before any treatment
questions.exp: The absolute neutrophil count is 6,000 x 0.004 = 24/microL: severe neutropenia. Fever with severe neutropenia is a medical emergency: take blood cultures and start IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour. Then investigate the cause (repeated counts for cyclic neutropenia, bone marrow, antineutrophil antibodies).

questions.question: A child is pale. Blood count shows low haemoglobin, low MCV and a high RDW. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Iron deficiency gives a microcytic anaemia with a HIGH RDW (red cells of different sizes) and a low ferritin. Thalassaemia trait gives a microcytosis that is out of proportion to the mild anaemia, a normal RDW, a high red cell count and a Mentzer index (MCV/RBC) under 13.

questions.question: A child has an abdominal mass, and examination shows hemihypertrophy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Hemihypertrophy (Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome, or isolated) raises the risk of embryonal tumours, especially Wilms tumour and hepatoblastoma. A smooth flank mass that does not cross the midline in a well child is typical of Wilms. Children with hemihypertrophy need abdominal ultrasound every 3 months until 7–8 years (and AFP for hepatoblastoma in BWS).

questions.question: In disseminated intravascular coagulation, how do fibrin degradation products (FDPs) make bleeding worse?
questions.e: They block fibrin polymerisation and platelet aggregation (an anticoagulant effect)
questions.exp: In DIC, widespread clotting uses up platelets and clotting factors, and fibrinolysis produces FDPs and D-dimers. FDPs interfere with fibrin monomer polymerisation and platelet function, adding to the bleeding. Treat the cause, and give platelets, FFP and cryoprecipitate (fibrinogen) if bleeding.

questions.question: Which result confirms beta-thalassaemia trait?
questions.exp: Beta-thalassaemia trait: mild microcytic anaemia with a normal ferritin and a raised HbA2 (3.5–7%) on electrophoresis or HPLC. Iron deficiency can lower HbA2, so correct iron first. HbH inclusions are seen in alpha-thalassaemia (HbH disease).

questions.question: A child has autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and immune thrombocytopenia together. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Evans syndrome is autoimmune destruction of two or more blood cell lines (Coombs-positive haemolytic anaemia with ITP, sometimes neutropenia). It is chronic and relapsing, and can be linked to immune dysregulation (ALPS, CVID) or lupus. Treat with steroids, IVIG and second-line immunosuppression.

questions.question: A child has acute haemolysis with a fast heart rate after a viral illness. A mass (the spleen) is felt in the left hypochondrium, the blood film shows spherocytes and the direct Coombs test is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Spherocytes are seen in both hereditary spherocytosis and AIHA; the positive direct Coombs test makes this AIHA. Children with sickle cell disease lose their spleen function early (autosplenectomy), and G6PD deficiency shows bite and blister cells with a negative Coombs test.

questions.question: A child with sickle cell disease comes to the emergency department with right upper quadrant pain. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Chronic haemolysis produces bilirubin (pigment) gallstones in up to 50% of children with sickle cell disease by adolescence, causing biliary colic and cholecystitis. Do an ultrasound; elective cholecystectomy is advised for symptomatic stones. Hepatic sequestration and sickle hepatopathy are rarer causes of RUQ pain, with a rapidly enlarging liver and falling Hb.

questions.question: A child has acute haemolysis after taking a sulfonamide drug. What is the definitive diagnostic test?
questions.exp: Oxidant drugs (sulfonamides, primaquine, nitrofurantoin), fava beans and infections trigger haemolysis in G6PD deficiency. The blood film shows bite and blister cells and Heinz bodies. Confirm with a quantitative G6PD assay; during an acute episode young red cells have more enzyme, giving a falsely normal result, so repeat it 2–3 months later if normal.

questions.question: A 3-year-old boy develops acute haemolysis with low Hb and high reticulocytes after eating fava beans. The direct Coombs test is negative. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Coombs-negative acute haemolysis after fava beans (favism) is G6PD deficiency, an X-linked disorder common in the Middle East. Haemolysis is intravascular (dark urine), with bite cells. Avoid triggers; transfuse if severe. A positive Coombs test would point to an immune cause.

questions.question: A child has progressive tiredness. Blood tests show a high white cell count, anaemia and thrombocytopenia, and there is generalised lymphadenopathy. What is the most diagnostic test?
questions.exp: Leukaemia (most often ALL) is suggested by two or more cell lines being abnormal, lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. A blood film may show blasts, but bone marrow aspiration (with immunophenotyping and cytogenetics) confirms and classifies it (more than 20–25% blasts). Get a chest X-ray before anaesthesia to look for a mediastinal mass.

questions.question: After a bout of gastroenteritis, a child has puffy eyelids and reduced urine. Tests show haemolysis (low Hb, high reticulocytes), thrombocytopenia and high urea and creatinine. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Typical HUS follows bloody diarrhoea from Shiga-toxin E. coli (O157:H7): microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (fragmented red cells, Coombs negative), thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury. Coagulation is usually normal (unlike DIC). Management is supportive (fluids, dialysis if needed); antibiotics and antimotility drugs should be avoided in STEC diarrhoea.

questions.question: A mother brings her son to the emergency department because his sibling died suddenly. What is the most appropriate next test for this child?
questions.e: A 12-lead ECG, with a full history and examination
questions.exp: Sudden cardiac death in a young relative may be due to an inherited condition: long QT, Brugada, catecholaminergic VT, WPW or cardiomyopathy. Screen siblings with a careful history (syncope, palpitations, family history) and examination, then a 12-lead ECG, plus echocardiography and exercise testing, and genetic testing if a cause is found.

questions.question: A child has tachycardia, tachypnoea, a gallop rhythm and an enlarged tender liver. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.exp: These are signs of congestive heart failure (fluid overload with hepatic congestion). First give a diuretic, oxygen and treatment of the cause. A fluid bolus would make it worse. Beta-blockers are started later for chronic heart failure, not in acute decompensation.

questions.question: An infant has tachycardia and tachypnoea. Three days ago he had fever and a runny nose. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Myocarditis often follows a viral illness (coxsackie B, adenovirus, parvovirus B19): unexplained tachycardia out of proportion to fever, tachypnoea, gallop rhythm, hepatomegaly and heart failure or shock. ECG shows low voltages and ST changes, troponin is raised, and the echo shows a poorly contracting, dilated left ventricle. Rheumatic fever is rare under 5 years.

questions.question: An infant has a heart rate of 260/min with a narrow QRS, pallor and no murmur. The rest of the examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: In infants, SVT is usually above 220/min, with a fixed rate, no beat-to-beat variation and absent or abnormal P waves. Sinus tachycardia is usually under 220/min and varies. Treat a stable child with vagal manoeuvres (ice to the face), then IV adenosine; synchronised cardioversion if shocked.

questions.question: A well child who is growing normally has a grade 2/6 systolic murmur at the upper left sternal border with an ejection click. The murmur does not change with position. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: An innocent murmur changes with position (softer when sitting or standing) and has no click. A murmur that does not change with posture, with an ejection click that varies with breathing, suggests pulmonary valve stenosis. Confirm with echocardiography; mild stenosis needs only follow-up, while moderate to severe stenosis is treated by balloon valvuloplasty.

questions.question: A child has supravalvular aortic stenosis with narrowing of the coronary artery origins. Which syndrome is most likely?
questions.exp: Williams syndrome (7q11.23 deletion including the elastin gene): elfin face, friendly "cocktail party" personality, intellectual disability, hypercalcaemia, and an elastin arteriopathy causing supravalvular aortic stenosis, peripheral pulmonary stenosis, coronary ostial stenosis and renal artery stenosis. Noonan has pulmonary stenosis; Turner has bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation.

questions.question: A child has had fever for 6 days with a rash, bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, a strawberry tongue and peeling of the fingers and toes. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Fever for 5 days or more with conjunctivitis, oral changes, rash, extremity changes and cervical lymphadenopathy is Kawasaki disease. Peeling of the fingertips starts in the second to third week. Scarlet fever has exudative tonsillitis and a sandpaper rash, toxic shock has hypotension, and measles has cough, coryza and Koplik spots.

questions.question: What is the treatment of choice for this child with Kawasaki disease?
questions.exp: IVIG 2 g/kg as one infusion, plus aspirin, ideally within the first 10 days, prevents most coronary aneurysms. Do an echocardiogram at diagnosis and at 2 and 6 weeks. Live vaccines are delayed for 11 months after IVIG.

questions.question: Which statement about lumbosacral myelomeningocele is correct?
questions.a: Hydrocephalus occurs in fewer than 10% of cases
questions.b: Bladder and bowel function are always normal
questions.c: No child with myelomeningocele can ever walk, even with support
questions.d: Most children develop hydrocephalus, and around 80% need a shunt
questions.exp: Myelomeningocele is usually linked to the Chiari II malformation, and 80–90% develop hydrocephalus (many need a VP shunt). Walking depends on the level: most children with low lumbar or sacral lesions walk, often with orthoses. Neurogenic bladder and bowel are almost universal. Most have normal or near-normal intelligence. Prevention: folic acid 400 micrograms before conception (5 mg if high risk).

questions.question: A child on an antiepileptic drug develops pancreatitis and raised liver enzymes. Which drug is most likely to be responsible?
questions.exp: Sodium valproate can cause pancreatitis (check amylase if abdominal pain and vomiting) and hepatotoxicity, which can be fatal, especially under 2 years, with polytherapy, or with mitochondrial disease (POLG, Alpers). Other side effects: weight gain, tremor, hair loss, thrombocytopenia, hyperammonaemia and teratogenicity.

questions.question: An adolescent girl has tachycardia, exophthalmos, weight loss and a goitre. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Graves disease (TSH-receptor stimulating antibodies) is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism in children, especially adolescent girls: goitre, weight loss, tremor, tachycardia, heat intolerance, falling school performance, and eye signs (exophthalmos, lid lag) that are specific to Graves. Treat with carbimazole (not propylthiouracil) and a beta-blocker for symptoms.

questions.question: Which test best tells familial short stature from constitutional delay of growth?
questions.e: Bone age (X-ray of the left hand and wrist)
questions.exp: Both are healthy short children growing at a normal rate. In familial short stature the bone age equals the chronological age, puberty comes on time and final height is short like the parents. In constitutional delay the bone age is delayed, puberty is late, and final height reaches the family target.

questions.question: A mother brings her 4-year-old daughter because she is short. Examination is otherwise normal, but her height velocity is 3 cm per year. What is the next step?
questions.c: Reassure; this growth rate is normal at 4 years
questions.d: Investigate, including bone age, thyroid function, IGF-1 and a karyotype
questions.exp: At 4 years a normal height velocity is about 6–7 cm a year; 3 cm a year is too slow at any age between 3 years and puberty (under about 4–5 cm per year). Slow growth needs investigation even if the child looks well: hypothyroidism, GH deficiency, coeliac disease, and in every short girl a karyotype for Turner syndrome, which may have few other signs.

questions.question: A girl has early breast enlargement and pubic hair. Which test distinguishes central (gonadotrophin-dependent) from peripheral precocious puberty?
questions.a: LH and FSH levels, ideally after GnRH stimulation
questions.exp: In central precocious puberty the hypothalamic-pituitary axis is active, so LH (and FSH) rise, especially after a GnRH (or GnRH analogue) stimulation test. In peripheral puberty (ovarian cyst or tumour, CAH, McCune–Albright, exogenous oestrogen) LH and FSH are suppressed. Central puberty needs an MRI brain (more so in boys and young girls); 17-OHP is checked for CAH.

questions.question: An adolescent boy has 2 days of gradually increasing pain and redness of one testis, with dysuria but no urethral discharge. The pain eases when the testis is lifted and the cremasteric reflex is present. What is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.c: Urine culture and a first-void urine NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhoea
questions.exp: Gradual onset, dysuria, relief on elevation (Prehn sign) and a present cremasteric reflex suggest epididymo-orchitis. In sexually active adolescents the common causes are Chlamydia and gonorrhoea (test first-void urine by NAAT); in younger boys, urinary pathogens. If testicular torsion cannot be excluded (sudden onset, high-riding testis, absent cremasteric reflex), explore surgically without waiting for tests.

questions.question: A child is seen with hair loss from repeatedly pulling out his hair (trichotillomania). Which statement is correct?
questions.a: It needs treatment with oral antifungals
questions.b: It belongs to the obsessive–compulsive and related disorders spectrum
questions.d: It is always a sign of child abuse
questions.e: It is a fungal infection of the scalp
questions.exp: Trichotillomania is a body-focused repetitive behaviour classed with obsessive–compulsive and related disorders (DSM-5). Patches have irregular shapes with broken hairs of different lengths, and the scalp is normal. Treat with habit-reversal behavioural therapy; swallowed hair can form a trichobezoar.

questions.question: A teenager presents with a deep vein thrombosis. His father and sibling had the same problem. What is the most likely cause?
questions.c: An inherited thrombophilia (such as factor V Leiden)
questions.exp: Venous thrombosis in a young person with an affected parent and sibling points to inherited thrombophilia: factor V Leiden (most common), prothrombin G20210A, or deficiency of protein C, protein S or antithrombin. Screen after the acute episode and counsel the family; also look for acquired risks (central lines, immobility, the pill, antiphospholipid antibodies).

questions.question: A mother is worried that her son's speech is delayed. His growth and examination are normal. What advice should she be given to help his speech?
questions.a: Repeat the word back to him correctly pronounced, without criticising
questions.b: Correct every mistake and make him repeat it
questions.d: Avoid talking to him until he speaks more
questions.e: Do not look at him when he is speaking
questions.exp: Parents help language by talking and reading with the child, face to face, and by modelling: repeating what the child says back correctly and expanding it ("car" → "yes, a red car"), without criticism. Finishing sentences or forcing repetition reduces the child's attempts. Always check hearing in speech delay.

questions.question: Three days after a scratch near the eye, a child has fever, swollen red eyelids, proptosis and painful, limited eye movements. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Proptosis, painful or limited eye movements, reduced vision or a relative afferent pupillary defect mean the infection is behind the orbital septum (orbital cellulitis), an emergency that can cause blindness, cavernous sinus thrombosis or a brain abscess. Admit, give IV antibiotics, get a CT of the orbits and sinuses, and involve ophthalmology and ENT. Preseptal cellulitis has lid swelling without these signs.

questions.question: What is an advantage of breast milk over cow's milk?
questions.a: It contains secretory IgA and other anti-infective factors
questions.d: It has a higher renal solute load
questions.exp: Breast milk contains secretory IgA, lactoferrin, lysozyme, white cells and oligosaccharides that protect against infection, has easily absorbed iron (despite a low amount), a lower protein and renal solute load, and is clean and at the right temperature. Its vitamin K and vitamin D are low, so babies need vitamin K at birth and vitamin D supplements.

questions.question: A mother asks which vitamin her baby needs if he is fed only on goat's milk. What is the answer?
questions.exp: Goat's milk is very low in folate (and B12), so babies fed only on it develop megaloblastic anaemia. It also has a high protein and electrolyte load and is not suitable as a main drink under 1 year. If used, folic acid supplements are needed.

questions.question: An infant drinks a lot of cow's milk and eats little solid food. What is the most likely problem?
questions.exp: Cow's milk is low in iron, reduces the appetite for iron-rich foods and can cause occult gut blood loss in infants, so excessive milk drinking (over about 500–600 mL a day) is the classic cause of iron deficiency anaemia in toddlers. Limit milk, give iron-rich foods and oral iron.

questions.question: An 8-year-old girl took unknown tablets and threw the packet away. Her heart rate is 50/min and her blood pressure is low-normal. She is drowsy and her blood glucose is low. Which drug is most likely?
questions.exp: Bradycardia, hypotension and hypoglycaemia suggest beta-blocker poisoning (treat with glucagon, glucose, atropine and high-dose insulin). Calcium channel blockers also cause bradycardia and hypotension, but usually HYPERglycaemia. Tricyclics and salbutamol cause tachycardia.

questions.question: A toddler drank toilet cleaner. He has vomited and is drooling with difficulty swallowing, although there are no visible mouth ulcers. What is the next step?
questions.d: Upper GI endoscopy as soon as possible (within 12–24 hours)
questions.e: Reassure, because there are no mouth burns
questions.exp: Caustic ingestion: the absence of mouth burns does not exclude oesophageal injury. Drooling, dysphagia, vomiting, stridor or chest pain predict significant injury and need endoscopy within 12–24 hours to grade the burns. Do not induce vomiting, neutralise or give charcoal. Late complication: oesophageal stricture.

questions.question: A child has abdominal pain for 3 days and comes to the emergency department with a dry mouth and urinary retention. Which medicine is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Anticholinergic effects: dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation, flushing, dilated pupils, tachycardia, and in overdose confusion ("dry as a bone, red as a beet, blind as a bat, mad as a hatter"). Hyoscine is an antimuscarinic antispasmodic often given for abdominal pain.

questions.question: A mother worries that her 4-year-old son has muscular dystrophy because he limps. His growth and examination are normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.exp: A serum CK is a simple, cheap screening test: it is very high (often over 10,000) in Duchenne muscular dystrophy from birth, even before weakness is obvious. A normal CK excludes DMD. Look also for a Gowers sign and calf hypertrophy, and for other causes of a limp.

questions.question: A girl fell from a height. She has severe left flank and abdominal pain and visible haematuria. What is the most likely injury?
questions.b: Renal injury (kidney laceration or renal pedicle injury)
questions.exp: Flank pain and haematuria after a fall or deceleration injury suggest a kidney injury; children's kidneys are relatively unprotected. A contrast CT grades the injury; most are managed without surgery. The spleen is also often injured with left-sided trauma, but haematuria points to the kidney.

questions.question: A boy with meningitis develops a seizure 2 days after admission. Which finding suggests the syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH)?
questions.a: Inappropriately high urine osmolality with low serum sodium
questions.exp: SIADH: hyponatraemia and low serum osmolality with an inappropriately concentrated urine (high urine osmolality and urine sodium), in a child who is not dehydrated. It complicates meningitis, pneumonia and head injury. Hyponatraemia can cause seizures. Restrict fluids; treat seizures from severe hyponatraemia with 3% saline.

questions.question: Which finding indicates tumour lysis syndrome?
questions.exp: Tumour lysis (mostly with Burkitt lymphoma and high-count ALL at the start of treatment) releases cell contents: HIGH uric acid, potassium and phosphate, and LOW calcium (bound by phosphate), with acute kidney injury. Prevent with hyperhydration and allopurinol or rasburicase.

questions.question: A girl comes to the emergency department with fever of 39°C, prolonged capillary refill and tachycardia. Her blood pressure is normal for her age. What is the most urgent problem?
questions.exp: Shock is inadequate tissue perfusion, not low blood pressure: tachycardia and prolonged capillary refill with fever mean compensated septic shock. Hypotension is a late sign in children. Give oxygen, IV/IO access, fluid boluses (10 mL/kg, reassess), blood cultures and antibiotics within an hour.

questions.question: Which of the following shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the LEFT?
questions.exp: A left shift means haemoglobin holds oxygen more tightly: HbF (binds 2,3-DPG poorly), alkalosis, low CO2, hypothermia, low 2,3-DPG and carbon monoxide. Acidosis, fever, high CO2 and high 2,3-DPG shift it to the right, releasing oxygen to the tissues (Bohr effect).

questions.question: A girl has global developmental delay, upslanting eyes, a flat back of the head (brachycephaly), epicanthic folds and a single palmar crease. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Down syndrome (trisomy 21): hypotonia, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthic folds, flat occiput and face, Brushfield spots, single palmar crease, sandal gap, and learning disability. Check for AVSD (echo), duodenal atresia, hypothyroidism, hearing and vision problems, and leukaemia risk.

questions.question: A boy has severe learning disability, like his brother. He has a long face, large ears, a prominent jaw and large testes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Fragile X (FMR1 CGG repeat expansion) is the most common inherited cause of learning disability: long face, large ears, prominent jaw, macro-orchidism after puberty, joint laxity, autism and ADHD features. Diagnose by FMR1 DNA testing; carrier mothers may have premature ovarian failure.

questions.question: A pedigree shows the disease in every generation, affecting both males and females, with male-to-male transmission. What is the inheritance?
questions.exp: Autosomal dominant: vertical transmission (every generation), both sexes equally, each child of an affected parent has a 50% risk, and male-to-male transmission occurs (which rules out X-linked). Autosomal recessive skips generations and is linked to consanguinity; mitochondrial passes only through mothers.

questions.question: A toddler has intermittent loose stools with undigested food but is growing well and is otherwise healthy. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Toddler's diarrhoea: 1–5-year-olds with loose stools containing undigested food (peas, carrots), often worse with fruit juice, but thriving with normal growth. It is caused by fast gut transit. Reassure; reduce juice and squash, normal fat and fibre intake. Investigate if growth falters.

questions.question: A child has failure to thrive, with height and weight below the 5th centile, and recurrent mouth ulcers. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Crohn's disease can involve the whole gut from mouth to anus: oral ulcers, growth failure and delayed puberty (often before gut symptoms), abdominal pain, diarrhoea, perianal disease and raised inflammatory markers. Ulcerative colitis affects only the colon and usually presents with bloody diarrhoea.

questions.question: Which factor increases the risk of cancer in ulcerative colitis?
questions.c: Young age at diagnosis without colonic involvement
questions.d: Involvement of the whole colon (pancolitis) and long disease duration
questions.exp: Colorectal cancer risk in UC rises with extensive disease (pancolitis), duration (from about 8–10 years), primary sclerosing cholangitis, and a family history. Children with extensive colitis start colonoscopic surveillance about 8 years after diagnosis. Mesalazine may lower the risk.

questions.question: An adolescent has mild unconjugated (indirect) hyperbilirubinaemia during an upper respiratory infection. Other liver tests and the blood count are normal. Gilbert syndrome is suspected. What is the next step?
questions.exp: Gilbert syndrome (reduced UGT1A1 activity) causes mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia that rises with fasting, illness or stress, with normal liver enzymes and no haemolysis. It is harmless and needs no treatment.

questions.question: Which test confirms the diagnosis of coeliac disease in a child with a positive anti-tTG?
questions.exp: Duodenal biopsy showing villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytes confirms coeliac disease, while still on gluten. ESPGHAN allows diagnosis without biopsy if anti-tTG IgA is over 10 times the upper limit and endomysial antibody is positive on a second sample.

questions.question: After surgery for Hirschsprung disease, a child has urinary incontinence from damage to the nerves supplying the bladder detrusor muscle. Which nerves were injured?
questions.exp: The detrusor contracts under parasympathetic control via the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4), which run close to the rectum and can be injured in pelvic dissection. Sympathetic hypogastric nerves (T10–L2) relax the detrusor and close the internal sphincter; the pudendal nerve supplies the external sphincter.

questions.question: What is the most common first presentation of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency in infancy?
questions.exp: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (PiZZ) is a common genetic cause of neonatal cholestasis (conjugated jaundice, pale stools, sometimes bleeding from vitamin K deficiency). It can progress to cirrhosis. Lung emphysema appears in adult life, made worse by smoking. Diagnose by serum level and phenotype.

questions.question: A neonate has bilious vomiting but has passed stool since birth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bilious vomiting in a newborn is a surgical emergency until proven otherwise, and malrotation with volvulus must be excluded first because the gut can die within hours. Passing stool does not exclude it. Pyloric stenosis and reflux cause non-bilious vomiting.

questions.question: What is the diagnostic test for suspected malrotation with volvulus in this neonate?
questions.e: Upper GI contrast study (showing the position of the duodenojejunal flexure)
questions.exp: An upper GI contrast study is the gold standard: the duodenojejunal flexure lies abnormally (right of the midline, low), with a corkscrew appearance in volvulus. Ultrasound may show reversed SMA/SMV relation or a whirlpool sign. Do not delay surgery (Ladd procedure) if the baby is unwell.

questions.question: A child has a severe egg allergy. Which vaccine still needs special precautions or specialist advice?
questions.exp: Influenza and MMR vaccines can be given normally to egg-allergic children (MMR is grown in chick fibroblasts with negligible egg protein; influenza vaccines have tiny ovalbumin amounts). Yellow fever vaccine contains more egg protein, so severe egg allergy needs specialist assessment before it is given.

questions.question: A sexually active adolescent boy has dysuria and a urethral discharge. Gram stain shows Gram-negative intracellular diplococci. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Gram-negative intracellular diplococci in a urethral smear confirm gonorrhoea. Chlamydia is often present too and is detected by NAAT. Test for other STIs (HIV, syphilis), and treat partners.

questions.question: An adolescent has a purulent urethral discharge. A sample is sent for culture. What is the appropriate empirical treatment while waiting for the result?
questions.a: Ceftriaxone plus treatment for chlamydia (doxycycline or azithromycin)
questions.d: No treatment until the culture result
questions.exp: Empirical treatment covers both gonorrhoea and chlamydia: a single IM dose of ceftriaxone plus doxycycline for 7 days (or azithromycin, used when doxycycline is not suitable). Quinolone resistance in gonorrhoea is common. Abstain from sex until treatment is complete; contact tracing.

questions.question: A child with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia has fever, and the blood culture grows Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Which antibiotic is the drug of choice?
questions.exp: Febrile neutropenia needs an anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam: piperacillin–tazobactam, ceftazidime, cefepime or meropenem (often with an aminoglycoside if unstable). Ceftriaxone, amoxicillin, vancomycin and clindamycin do not reliably cover Pseudomonas.

questions.question: A child has fever, looks ill and has a fast heart rate. What is the initial treatment?
questions.a: Wait for blood results before treating
questions.b: Intravenous fluid bolus with antibiotics after cultures
questions.exp: An ill-looking febrile child with tachycardia may have sepsis. Give oxygen, get IV/IO access, take cultures, give a 10 mL/kg crystalloid bolus (reassess) and broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour. Antipyretics do not treat the cause.

questions.question: A child has perianal itching at night, and pinworms (Enterobius vermicularis) are seen. What is the treatment?
questions.e: Mebendazole once, repeated after 2 weeks, treating the whole household
questions.exp: Threadworms: a single dose of mebendazole (over 6 months of age) kills adult worms, repeated after 2 weeks to catch newly hatched worms; treat all household members at the same time. Hygiene (hand washing, short nails, morning bath, washing bedding) prevents reinfection. Diagnose with the sticky tape test.

questions.question: A child has a gluteal abscess over 2 cm, which has been incised and drained of pus. Which antibiotic is appropriate to cover community-acquired MRSA?
questions.exp: Incision and drainage is the main treatment for skin abscesses. Antibiotics are added for large abscesses (over 2 cm), surrounding cellulitis, systemic signs or immunosuppression. Where community-acquired MRSA is common, use clindamycin or co-trimoxazole; flucloxacillin or cefalexin cover only MSSA.

questions.question: An immunocompromised child has been in contact with a sibling who has measles. What is the prophylaxis of choice?
questions.exp: Immunocompromised children cannot receive live MMR vaccine and are at risk of severe measles (pneumonitis, encephalitis). Give human normal immunoglobulin (IVIG) within 6 days of exposure. Healthy unvaccinated contacts over 6 months can have MMR within 72 hours.

questions.question: An abandoned neonate is tested. All antibody tests are negative except HIV and rubella antibodies. What is the appropriate next step?
questions.b: Treat for HIV straight away based on antibodies alone
questions.c: HIV DNA (or RNA) PCR on the baby's blood
questions.exp: Maternal IgG antibodies cross the placenta and can last up to 18 months, so a positive HIV antibody test in an infant shows only exposure. Infection is diagnosed by HIV nucleic acid tests (DNA or RNA PCR) at birth, 6 weeks and 3 months. Start ART prophylaxis while waiting.

questions.question: A pregnant woman is HIV positive. What is the best way to prevent transmission to her baby?
questions.a: Avoid all testing of the baby
questions.b: Antiretroviral therapy for the mother throughout pregnancy, then infant antiretroviral prophylaxis
questions.c: Induce labour at 38 weeks without treatment
questions.d: Reassure the mother; transmission is rare without treatment
questions.exp: Maternal ART started as early as possible to suppress the viral load reduces transmission to under 1%. The baby gets antiretroviral prophylaxis (zidovudine or combination if high risk) from birth. Elective caesarean section is considered if the viral load is not suppressed; avoid breastfeeding where formula is safe.

questions.question: A child with fever, altered behaviour and seizures has a lumbar puncture showing a lymphocytic CSF. What is the next step?
questions.b: Repeat lumbar puncture in a week
questions.c: Stop treatment if the CSF glucose is normal
questions.e: CSF PCR for herpes simplex virus, while starting IV aciclovir
questions.exp: Encephalitis (fever, altered consciousness, seizures, focal signs) with lymphocytic CSF needs HSV PCR and immediate IV aciclovir (do not wait for the result). MRI shows temporal lobe changes and EEG periodic discharges. A negative early PCR may need repeating.

questions.question: A girl visited her grandfather's farm, milked cows, fed chickens and rode camels. She now has fever and hepatosplenomegaly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Brucellosis follows contact with farm animals (cows, goats, sheep, camels) or unpasteurised milk: undulant fever, sweats, arthralgia, hepatosplenomegaly. Blood culture (prolonged incubation) and serology. Treat with combined antibiotics for at least 6 weeks.

questions.question: A child with glycogen storage disease has frequent hypoglycaemia. What helps prevent hypoglycaemia at night?
questions.d: Uncooked cornstarch at bedtime (or continuous overnight feeds)
questions.exp: In GSD type I the liver cannot release glucose, so fasting causes hypoglycaemia with lactic acidosis. Uncooked cornstarch is slowly digested and keeps glucose steady for several hours; young infants need frequent or continuous feeds. Avoid fructose and galactose in type I.

questions.question: A child has hypoglycaemia with no metabolic acidosis and no ketones in the urine. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Hypoketotic hypoglycaemia means fats cannot be turned into ketones (fatty acid oxidation defects such as MCAD) or ketone production is suppressed by insulin (hyperinsulinism). MCAD presents after fasting or illness, often 3–24 months; check acylcarnitines. Avoid fasting and give glucose when ill.

questions.question: A preterm baby has respiratory distress, and the chest X-ray shows a ground-glass appearance with air bronchograms. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: RDS: preterm babies with grunting, recession and rising oxygen need; X-ray shows a diffuse ground-glass (reticulogranular) pattern, air bronchograms and low lung volumes. Treat with CPAP and surfactant. Antenatal steroids reduce it.

questions.question: A baby is born through thick meconium-stained liquor and is not breathing. What is the appropriate intervention?
questions.a: Intubate and suction the trachea before any breath
questions.c: Stimulate for 2 minutes before doing anything else
questions.e: Start positive pressure ventilation; routine tracheal suction is not recommended
questions.exp: Current newborn resuscitation guidance (NRP 8th edition, Resuscitation Council UK) no longer recommends routine intubation and tracheal suction for non-vigorous babies born through meconium, because it delays ventilation. Open the airway and start inflation breaths; suction only if the airway is obstructed.

questions.question: A term baby born by caesarean section has respiratory distress from birth. The chest X-ray shows fluid in the horizontal fissure. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: TTN: delayed clearance of lung fluid, more common after caesarean section without labour. Tachypnoea for 24–72 hours, a chest X-ray with fluid in the fissures, perihilar streaking and hyperinflation. Supportive care with oxygen or CPAP; it resolves in 1–3 days.

questions.question: A breastfed baby delivered at home bleeds from the umbilical stump. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Breast milk is low in vitamin K, and babies born at home may miss the vitamin K injection, so they are at risk of vitamin K deficiency bleeding (PT prolonged). Prevent with 1 mg IM vitamin K at birth.

questions.question: A neonate has poor feeding, lethargy and a high ammonia, with no metabolic acidosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Hyperammonaemia without acidosis (often with respiratory alkalosis) is typical of urea cycle defects such as OTC deficiency. Organic acidaemias cause hyperammonaemia with a high anion gap acidosis.

questions.question: A newborn on day 3 has poor feeding, lethargy and a high ammonia from a suspected urea cycle defect. What is the most appropriate first step?
questions.a: Stop protein feeds and start IV 10% dextrose with electrolytes
questions.b: Wait for genetic results before treating
questions.exp: Emergency management of hyperammonaemia: stop all protein, give IV 10% dextrose (with saline) at high rates to stop catabolism (insulin if hyperglycaemic), start ammonia scavengers (sodium benzoate, sodium phenylbutyrate) and arginine, and arrange haemodialysis if ammonia is very high (over about 250–500 micromol/L) or rising.

questions.question: A full-term neonate weighs 1.2 kg, with weight and length below the 10th centile but a head circumference on the 50th centile. What is the most likely cause?
questions.d: Maternal hypertension (placental insufficiency) in the third trimester
questions.e: Congenital infection in the first trimester
questions.exp: Asymmetric growth restriction with head sparing comes from late-pregnancy placental insufficiency (pre-eclampsia, hypertension, smoking), where blood is redirected to the brain. Symmetric restriction (head also small) starts early: congenital infection (CMV), chromosomal disorders, drugs or alcohol. These babies are at risk of hypoglycaemia, hypothermia and polycythaemia.

questions.question: A mother had prolonged rupture of membranes and is known to carry group B streptococcus. Her baby is unwell at birth. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: GBS is the leading cause of early-onset neonatal sepsis (within 72 hours, often in the first 12): respiratory distress, apnoea, poor perfusion, temperature instability, pneumonia and meningitis. Risk factors: maternal GBS carriage, prolonged rupture of membranes, maternal fever, prematurity. Give intrapartum antibiotics to colonised mothers; treat the baby with IV benzylpenicillin and gentamicin.

questions.question: A neonate has bilious vomiting, and the X-ray shows a double bubble. Which condition is most strongly associated?
questions.exp: A double bubble (dilated stomach and duodenum) means duodenal atresia or stenosis, or an annular pancreas; vomiting is bilious when the block is below the ampulla. About 30% of babies with duodenal atresia have Down syndrome. Treat with gastric decompression, fluids and duodenoduodenostomy.

questions.question: A 10-year-old with a past history of asthma has had a cough for a few months. It happens all day, sounds loud and honking, and never happens at night or during sleep. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: A habit or psychogenic (somatic) cough is a loud, honking or barking cough that disappears during sleep and when distracted, often starting after a respiratory infection. Asthma cough is typically worse at night and with exercise. Treat with suggestion therapy and behavioural approaches; avoid escalating asthma drugs.

questions.question: A 7-year-old has an afebrile cough without respiratory distress. He looks well, but the chest X-ray shows bilateral infiltrates. What is the appropriate antibiotic?
questions.exp: Mycoplasma pneumoniae ("walking pneumonia") is common in school-age children: gradual onset, headache, malaise, persistent cough, few signs and an X-ray worse than the child looks. Beta-lactams do not work (no cell wall); give a macrolide such as azithromycin (or doxycycline over 8 years).

questions.question: A child has a barking cough, stridor, drooling of saliva, high fever and looks toxic. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Epiglottitis (Haemophilus influenzae type b, now rare after vaccination): sudden high fever, toxic look, drooling, muffled voice, sitting forward (tripod), soft stridor, usually little cough. Do not examine the throat or upset the child; call a senior anaesthetist and ENT to secure the airway, then IV ceftriaxone. A barking cough with a toxic child also suggests bacterial tracheitis, so keep it in mind.

questions.question: A teenager wants to play competitive sport and asks for screening to rule out hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. What is the basic screening approach?
questions.a: A careful history (including family history of sudden death) and examination, with a 12-lead ECG
questions.exp: Pre-participation screening: personal symptoms (exertional chest pain, syncope, palpitations), family history of sudden cardiac death under 50 or cardiomyopathy, and examination (murmur louder with Valsalva or standing in HCM, Marfan features). Many programmes add a 12-lead ECG. Echocardiography follows if anything is abnormal.

questions.question: A child with juvenile idiopathic arthritis takes an NSAID long term and develops a peptic ulcer. How do NSAIDs cause this?
questions.a: By reducing gastric prostaglandin production (COX-1 inhibition)
questions.d: By increasing gastrin secretion from a tumour
questions.exp: Prostaglandins protect the stomach lining (mucus and bicarbonate secretion, blood flow). NSAIDs block COX-1, reducing them and causing gastritis and ulcers. Give the NSAID with food, use the lowest dose, and add a proton pump inhibitor if long-term treatment is needed.

questions.question: A teenager has persistent mild jaundice. The bilirubin is mainly CONJUGATED, and liver enzymes are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Dubin–Johnson syndrome (MRP2 defect, autosomal recessive) causes benign, lifelong conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with normal enzymes and a dark, pigmented liver. Rotor syndrome is similar without pigment. Gilbert and Crigler–Najjar cause UNCONJUGATED hyperbilirubinaemia.
